performers: Constance Schoepflin, flute; Advent Chamber Orchestra
intro: Constance Schoepflin and the Advent Chamber Orchestra play the Presto finale of C. P. E. Bach’s Flute Concerto in G major, Wq 169 / H 445. The flute begins with the strings, then plays trills and long runs alone.

sections.label: A · Opening theme, G major, flute and strings
sections.mNote: The whole ensemble plays the opening G major theme.

sections.label: B · Flute solo entry
sections.mNote: The opening tune returns with an added trill and slur

sections.label: C · Flute runs and string replies
sections.mNote: Long solo phrases alternate with shorter orchestral passages

sections.label: D · Fermata over D
sections.mNote: The flute holds G above D in the bass.

sections.label: E · Opening theme, flute and strings
sections.mNote: Flute and strings play the rising figure again

sections.label: A′ · Final tutti in G major
sections.mNote: The flute joins strings and bass for the final tutti.

cues.title: Opening of the Presto
cues.text: The Presto begins with a short rising scale, clipped notes and a trill. Flute and strings share the tune, and the bass has running notes of its own. The dynamics switch quickly between piano and forte.
cues.evidence: Critical performing parts, flute and basso, Presto bars 1–48, PDF pp. 21–22. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First flute solo
cues.text: In its first solo the flute plays the opening tune with a trill on the pickup G and a slur across the bar line. The strings accompany.
cues.evidence: First solo at bar 49, critical flute part, PDF p. 22. Kuijken discusses the added trill and slur in the edition’s introduction. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf ; https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Organ concerto arranged for flute
cues.text: Bach first wrote this concerto for organ in 1755. To make a flute version, he raised low passages, changed others and left room for breathing.
cues.evidence: Barthold Kuijken, introduction to Wq 169: organ original Wq 34, dated 1755; flute adaptation made before 1768, with changes to range and breathing. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Court appointment, Charlottenburg, 1740
cues.text: In 1740, at Charlottenburg, Bach accompanied Frederick II in his first flute solo after his accession. The king’s new harpsichordist was twenty-six. At the Prussian court, flute playing was part of his daily professional work.
cues.evidence: Bach’s autobiographical account, quoted in The Essential C. P. E. Bach, introduction, p. xviii; the court appointment begins in 1740. https://www.cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/Essential-CPEB-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Manuscript P 769, Berlin
cues.text: A copyist, identified by Kuijken as Anon. 303, wrote out the keyboard concerto and left the top staff empty. Bach filled it with a flute part in his own hand and then changed the accompaniment. The manuscript is in Berlin, Mus. ms. Bach P 769.
cues.evidence: Kuijken identifies copyist Anon. 303 and Bach’s autograph additions in Berlin manuscript Mus. ms. Bach P 769. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Fermata, bar 236
cues.text: The running flute line reaches a fermata in bar 236, holding G above D in the bass. The violins and viola rest. After the held note Bach writes a short turn and the descent to the returning tune at bar 237.
cues.evidence: Presto bar 236 and return at 237: flute, PDF p. 27; resting upper strings, pp. 42, 56 and 69; basso fermata, p. 84. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Inserted orchestral bars, finale
cues.text: Late in the finale, Bach inserted three bars that do not appear in the organ version. The flute rests while the strings play, and then the soloist starts another long run. Kuijken identifies these bars, 287–89 of the Presto, as a place for the flautist to breathe.
cues.evidence: Kuijken identifies the inserted orchestral intervention at Presto bars 287–89 as a breathing opportunity. This note concerns the adaptation, not a timed entry. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

cues.title: Closing tutti
cues.text: In the final tutti the flute plays the ensemble’s tune. Trills, slurred pairs and repeated high notes lead to the close, where flute, strings and bass end together on G major.
cues.evidence: Closing tutti, bars 314–335: flute, PDF p. 29; first violin, p. 43; basso, p. 85. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Flute solo entry with trilled pickup
transitions.from: A · Opening theme, G major, flute and strings
transitions.how: The opening ensemble passage closes in G major. In bars 47–50 the flute plays the rising theme alone, with a trill on the pickup G and a slur across the bar line. Strings and bass accompany more softly beneath it. The tempo remains Presto.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 47–50, critical flute part, PDF p. 22; Kuijken’s introduction discusses the solo ornament. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf ; https://cpebach.org/pdfs/introductions/III-FS-Wq169-Intro.pdf

transitions.title: Flute run halts over held D
transitions.from: C · Flute runs and string replies
transitions.how: The flute plays descending semiquavers above repeated D notes in the bass. The run stops at a fermata, where the flute holds G above the bass’s held D. The violins and viola rest. The figured bass marks a suspended fourth resolving to a third, and the G major theme then returns.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 233–237: flute and figured bass, PDF p. 27; upper-string rests, pp. 42, 56 and 69; basso, p. 84. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

transitions.title: From the fermata to the return
transitions.to: E · Opening theme, flute and strings
transitions.how: After the held D in the bass, a low G marks the return. The flute’s pickup leads into the opening scale, now shared with the violins. Viola and bass resume their moving parts under the forte ensemble. The metre stays in two-four and the tempo stays Presto.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 236–240, flute, PDF p. 27; first violin, p. 42; viola, p. 69; basso, p. 84. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

transitions.title: Flute and tutti in the final cadence
transitions.from: E · Opening theme, flute and strings
transitions.to: A′ · Final tutti in G major
transitions.how: The solo flute’s running line gives way to a tutti, marked forte in the strings and bass. Slurred pairs and repeated high notes return from the opening. The bass moves through the closing phrases to a final D–G cadence, and the flute plays with the strings in the G major ending.
transitions.evidence: Presto bars 314–335: flute, PDF p. 29; first violin, p. 43; basso, p. 85. https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf

source.title: C. P. E. Bach, flute-concerto working score, Mus. ms. Bach P 769
source.locator: Presto, manuscript PDF pp. 11–39. Critical performing parts supply the flute’s ensemble passages: https://cpebach.org/pdfs/parts/Wq169-flute-parts.pdf, pp. 21–29. The fermata and string rests appear on pp. 27, 42, 56, 69 and 84. The cello desk represents the written basso part.

timeline.note: The flute plays the opening tune with the strings and bass, with quick piano and forte replies.
The flute adds a trill and slur to the opening theme; strings and bass accompany its first solo.
Long flute runs alternate with shorter string phrases above the moving bass.
At the fermata, the flute holds G above D in the bass. Violins and viola rest.
Flute and violins return to the opening rising figure, with viola and bass moving below them.
The closing tutti joins flute, strings and bass in the final G major cadence.

fields.note: Both sources name the soloist and ensemble. The opened programme does not identify a conductor for this concerto or its continuo player. Credits for soloists in the adjacent Brandenburg concertos have not been transferred to this track. Exact string numbers, keyboard type, double-bass participation and tuning are unestablished.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Flute version of the concerto; complete finale only
fields.note: Only movement III is hosted in this package. Set metadata records part 3 of 3, not possession of the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo. The 1755 date belongs to the original organ concerto Wq 34; the flute adaptation is later and cannot be assigned a precise year. The working manuscript is dated between 1755 and 1768 by Kuijken. The recording’s performing edition, any restored missing bar and the details of a cadenza are unestablished. The modern critical performing parts clarify the manuscript’s shorthand: flute participates in the opening and closing tutti, so a blank flute staff does not establish a rest. These parts are consulted as a reference, not attributed to the 2008 performance or claimed to be public domain. The score-derived orchestra display uses passage overviews rather than aligned entries; the cello desk represents written basso, not a verified allocation of bass instruments.

composer.epithet: Accompanist to Frederick the Great and composer of keyboard music known for abrupt interruptions and trembling single notes.
facts: His father, Johann Sebastian Bach; studied law in Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Frederick II’s harpsichordist, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88
Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, 1753 and 1762
Wq: Alfred Wotquenne · H: E. Eugene Helm

quote.text: A musician can move others only if he is moved himself.
quote.source: Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments, Part I, chapter 3, §13 (1753); our translation

composer.background:
On 12 October 1772, Charles Burney dined with Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach in Hamburg. Bach’s wife, his lawyer son, his daughter and three or four friends were present; upstairs was a music room hung with pictures, drawings and prints of more than a hundred and fifty musicians. Before dinner Bach had played his Silbermann clavichord; after dinner Burney persuaded him to return to the keyboard, and he played until nearly eleven. As he played, his eyes became fixed and his lower lip dropped. Burney wrote that on a long note Bach could draw from the clavichord “a cry of sorrow and complaint”.

Emanuel was born in Weimar on 8 March 1714, the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara. Telemann was his godfather. The household moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, when Sebastian became Thomaskantor. Visiting musicians came to play for his father; the boy heard them at home. “In composition and keyboard playing I never had any teacher other than my father,” he wrote in the autobiography published in 1773.
